subject: Post-call: workload mix, concurrency, and streaming clarifications
messages:
From: Samir Patel <samir@atlas-retail.com>
To: stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai; marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Sun, 18 May 2025 14:12:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery call recap — peak vs steady-state and streaming needs

Thanks for the call earlier — quick recap + a few clarifying details from our side so you can size more accurately. Appreciate the time.

Summary of our workload (from our instrumentation team):
- Average peak storefront traffic: ~420 concurrent sessions during campaigns (10% of global traffic window).
- Typical steady-state storefront sessions: ~45 concurrent.
- Typical QPS to generation endpoint: 75 QPS steady, spikes to ~1,100 QPS for 6-12 minute windows on campaign launches.
- Median tokens per request (user message): 220 tokens; responses average 350 tokens.
- We plan to enable streaming for the product recommendation flow — client expects ~200–300ms chunk cadence for UI updates (partial tokens streamed).

Questions for you:
1) Should we size using peak QPS or use a hybrid peak+burst model?
2) What's realistic 95th percentile latency for streaming partials at 300ms cadence vs full-response latency?
3) Are there specific batching/connection limits we should anticipate for concurrency per GPU?

I've attached our light workload snapshot CSV (atlas_workload_snapshot_May18.csv) with per-window samples. Looking for a short proposal for committed capacity + guardband and a suggested SLO approach.

—Samir
Customer Engineering, Atlas Retail

---
Attachment: atlas_workload_snapshot_May18.csv (3.2 KB, CSV summary)

From: stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai
To: Samir Patel <samir@atlas-retail.com>
Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 19 May 2025 09:03:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery call recap — peak vs steady-state and streaming needs

Samir — thanks, this is very helpful. A few quick clarifications before we draft sizing + SLO options: 

- Confirming the 1,100 QPS spike is sustained for 6–12 minutes per event and occurs roughly 2–3 times/week?
- For streaming cadence, when you say 200–300ms chunk cadence, is that for UI-level partials (best-effort) or a hard timing requirement (i.e., must be <=300ms 95% of the time)?
- Any per-user concurrency expectations — how many parallel open streaming sessions might a single end user have? (We typically assume 1–2, but some workflows open 3–4 tabs.)

Next steps we propose:
1) Marissa will draft a capacity sketch (reserved GPUs + burst policy) using two sizing models: conservative peak-pinned and hybrid burst with autoscale.
2) Karthik will outline the streaming behavior trade-offs (chunk size vs latency SLOs and how prefix/KV caching affects partial latency).
3) We’ll return a short SLO proposal (95th/99th latency targets for partials and full responses) and an ops checklist for campaign days.

Can you confirm answers to the three bullets above? If yes, we will aim to get the draft by EOD Tuesday PST.

Thanks — Steph
Steph Nguyen
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

From: marissa_cole@redwood.ai
To: Samir Patel <samir@atlas-retail.com>, stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Mon, 19 May 2025 13:46:00 -0700
Subject: RE: Discovery call recap — throughput and SLO sketch

Samir — looping in a rough throughput sketch and immediate asks (see attached PDF). High level recommendations below; we kept two scenarios so you can compare economics and risk.

Scenario A — Conservative (peak-pinned):
- Commit to reserved capacity sized for 1,200 QPS sustained peak guard (10% headroom on your 1,100 QPS spikes).
- This maps to ~6 dedicated A100-equivalent GPUs for model serving (assuming 4-6k tokens/sec per GPU depending on quantization).
- Latency targets: 95th full-response <= 450ms; streaming partials 95th <= 350ms (with warm KV cache).

Scenario B — Hybrid burst + autoscale (recommended for cost-sensitive ops):
- Reserved steady capacity for 120 QPS (~1 GPU) + autoscale pool that adds burst capacity up to 1,400 QPS for short windows.
- Autoscale warm-up policy: pre-warm burst when campaign TTL detected (API trigger or cron) — required to hit streaming partial SLOs.
- Latency targets: 95th full-response <= 550ms under burst; streaming partials best-effort 300ms cadence when warm, up to 800ms cold.

Concurrency & batching notes:
- We assume 1.5 concurrent requests per active session on average; for client-side parallelism of 3 tabs, plan for 3x per-user concurrency spikes.
- Effective tokens/sec per GPU will vary by sequence length; use the attached CSV to map tokens/sec distribution — we recommend a 25% headroom on token throughput to avoid queueing during peaks.

Next steps / asks from Atlas:
1) Confirm frequency of campaign spikes (2–3x/week vs daily).
2) Confirm whether 300ms streaming partials is a hard SLO or a UX guideline — affects pre-warm policy and cost.
3) Share any retention rules for KV/cache between requests (session stickiness).

Attachments: redwood_slo_proposal_v1.pdf (SLO options + cost delta table)

We’ll convert Scenario B into concrete commit vs burst numbers once we have the campaign cadence. If you want, we can also run a short traffic replay test in a sandbox to validate latencies for your 220-token inputs — that usually helps reduce the guardband.

—Marissa
Solutions Lead, Redwood Inference

From: Samir Patel <samir@atlas-retail.com>

Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, Taylor Huang <taylor@atlas-retail.com>
Date: Tue, 20 May 2025 09:28:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery call recap — throughput and SLO clarifications

Thanks team — this is excellent context and very actionable. Quick confirmations: 
- Campaign cadence: 2x/week on average, sometimes daily during holidays. Spikes are almost always 6–12 minutes and are predictable.
- Streaming partials: target is UX-driven — we want 300ms cadence for 95% of partial updates during warm/baseline conditions. Cold starts can be looser.
- Per-user concurrency: usually 1, rarely 2; we will surface 3+ tabs as an edge case and likely throttle at the client.

Please proceed with Scenario B draft (hybrid burst) and include a recommended pre-warm trigger (webhook + 5 min lookahead) and a sample ops runbook for campaign days. We are open to a small committed baseline if it materially reduces p95 partial latency.

Samir
Customer Engineering, Atlas Retail
